case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Louisiana's Healthcare Emergency Powers Act (LHEPA), a state COVID-19 emergency immunity statute, can lawfully displace or preempt federal disability discrimination claims brought under Title III of the ADA and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act by imposing a heightened gross negligence standard not required under federal law.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Louisiana Healthcare Emergency Powers Act (LHEPA); Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act (42 U.S.C. § 12182); Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 (29 U.S.C. § 794); Supremacy Clause, U.S. Const. Art. VI, cl. 2
case_analysis.petitioner_position: John Doe argues that the Louisiana courts improperly applied LHEPA's heightened gross negligence standard to his federal ADA and RA disability discrimination claims, effectively nullifying federally guaranteed civil rights protections through a state emergency immunity statute. He contends this constitutes unconstitutional displacement of federal law under the Supremacy Clause, creates dangerous precedent allowing states to conditionally suspend federal civil rights protections during declared emergencies, and produces absurd results by treating a federal civil rights claim as if it were a state tort or medical malpractice action. Petitioner further argues the case presents a pure, first-impression question of federal law warranting Supreme Court review.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Dynamic Physical Therapy and Scott Newton argue that the Petition rests on a false premise because monetary emotional distress damages are categorically unavailable to private plaintiffs under Title III of the ADA and Section 504 of the RA, citing Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, P.L.L.C. (596 U.S.). Respondents contend that LHEPA's application was appropriate given that the denial of aquatic physical therapy occurred in December 2020 during an active public health emergency, that Petitioner's preemption arguments were conclusory and unsupported by legal authority, and that the lower courts correctly found the allegations, even if accepted as true, failed to establish actionable conduct under the applicable legal standard, warranting dismissal for no cause of action.
key_precedents: Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, P.L.L.C., 596 U.S. (holding emotional distress damages unavailable under Section 504 of the RA)
Doe v. Dynamic Physical Therapy, LLC, 407 So.3d 623 (La. 2025) (Louisiana Supreme Court writ denial with Griffin dissent)
Mills v. Hartford Healthcare Corp., 347 A.3d 605, 619-20 (2023) (COVID-19 immunity statute analysis)
Resurgens, LLC v. Ervin, 894 S.E.2d 408, 411 (2023) (state COVID immunity interpretation)
Americans with Disabilities Act, Title III (42 U.S.C. § 12182)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas's most pointed challenge — that the preemption argument 'collapses at its foundation' if no cognizable federal remedy exists, and that the injunctive relief avenue may not have been properly preserved below — deserves serious engagement, but I find it ultimately insufficient to change my position. The record question he raises about preservation is a vehicle concern, not a merits concern, and if anything counsels a narrow GVR rather than affirmance for Respondent. Justice Barrett's movement toward Petitioner, despite her textualist caution, confirms that the Felder v. Casey structural argument is sound: a state law that alters the operative elements of a federal cause of action — what a plaintiff must prove, not merely what damages flow from proof — is preempted regardless of remedial constraints imposed by Cummings. As Chief Justice, I would assign the majority opinion with a formulation that holds only that LHEPA cannot displace the federal standard of liability for ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims, explicitly reserving the damages question under Cummings for remand, which should hold the 7-justice coalition together while avoiding any broader pronouncement about state emergency powers that would unnecessarily constrain future cases involving genuinely different factual circumstances.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan's invocation of Felder v. Casey is the strongest argument against my position, and I have genuinely wrestled with it — Felder's holding that state procedural requirements cannot burden the vindication of federally guaranteed rights does have structural resonance with LHEPA's imposition of a heightened fault standard. However, Felder involved a fully cognizable § 1983 damages claim where the federal remedy was unambiguously available; the structural parallel breaks down here because the federal remedy landscape is genuinely uncertain. Justice Gorsuch acknowledges the threshold concern directly — we cannot assume a preemption problem without identifying a cognizable federal remedy being obstructed — and the record does not clearly establish that injunctive relief under Title III was properly preserved and pursued below, which is not a technicality but a substantive limitation on our ability to reach the Supremacy Clause question. Justice Alito's mootness point reinforces my concern: where the alleged discriminatory conduct occurred during a discrete, concluded emergency event, the prospective nature of Title III injunctive relief is itself questionable, and this Court should not resolve a broad structural preemption question on a vehicle where the 'live controversy' premise rests on an unexamined and potentially defective foundation. The seven-justice majority's position is not without merit, but the institutional practice of avoiding broad constitutional pronouncements on underdeveloped records — which Justice Barrett herself acknowledges — counsels that this case is a poor vehicle regardless of the theoretical force of the Felder analogy.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan's invocation of Felder v. Casey is the strongest argument against my position, and I must engage with it directly: Felder held that a state procedural requirement was preempted as applied to § 1983 claims because it burdened the vindication of federal rights, and the structural parallel to LHEPA's heightened fault standard has genuine force. However, my textualist methodology requires me to identify a concrete, viable federal remedy actually being obstructed on these specific facts — and Justice Thomas correctly notes that the record does not clearly establish that the injunctive relief avenue was properly preserved and pursued below, making this a poor vehicle for the broad structural holding my colleagues propose. Even accepting that Title III injunctive relief survives Cummings in theory, the mootness concern I identified in Round 1 retains force: where the discriminatory conduct occurred during a discrete, concluded emergency event, the prospective nature of injunctive relief is itself questionable, and we should not resolve sweeping Supremacy Clause questions on a record that may not present a live injunctive controversy. I maintain my position for Respondent, though I acknowledge the 7-2 tally reflects that my colleagues find the Felder analogy more persuasive than I do, and I would write separately to flag the vehicle concerns Justice Thomas and I share.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas's most serious challenge — that the preemption argument collapses if no cognizable federal remedy exists — has been thoroughly addressed by the convergence of reasoning from Justices Kagan, Gorsuch, and Kavanaugh: Cummings constrains the remedial question but does not extinguish the federal cause of action, and Title III's injunctive relief preserves a live controversy sufficient to reach the Supremacy Clause issue. Justice Alito's mootness concern about prospective injunctive relief deserves acknowledgment, but it proves too much — if accepted, it would allow states to insulate discrete emergency conduct from any federal civil rights scrutiny simply by ensuring the emergency ends before litigation concludes, which cannot be the law. I am persuaded by Justice Roberts's narrowing instinct and would join an opinion holding only that LHEPA cannot alter the operative standard of liability for federal ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims, explicitly reserving the damages question for remand consistent with Cummings — this formulation maintains the structural integrity of federal antidiscrimination law while respecting legitimate state emergency authority and avoiding unnecessary constitutional breadth. The practical stakes for disabled individuals during emergencies, when they are most vulnerable and most dependent on federal civil rights protections, reinforce that the Supremacy Clause cannot permit states to conditionally rewrite the elements of federal anti-discrimination claims through emergency immunity statutes.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas's most serious challenge — that preemption must be tethered to a concrete federal right being displaced, and that the injunctive relief avenue may not have been properly preserved below — deserves direct engagement. But I find it ultimately unpersuasive for two reasons: first, the vehicle concern goes to whether this is the right case, not whether the legal principle is sound, and we regularly resolve questions of law even when the record is imperfect if the issue is squarely presented; second, and more fundamentally, Justice Barrett's movement toward the Petitioner position based on Felder v. Casey confirms that the structural preemption argument has genuine doctrinal grounding independent of the damages question. Justice Alito's mootness concern about injunctive relief for past discrete events has more bite than I initially credited — if the emergency has ended and no prospective relief is available, the live controversy premise weakens considerably — but this is a fact-specific inquiry that should be resolved on remand rather than used to foreclose the legal question entirely. I maintain my position that LHEPA cannot alter the operative liability standard for federal ADA and RA claims, consistent with Chief Justice Roberts's narrowing approach, while acknowledging that the precise scope of available injunctive relief on these facts requires careful remand consideration.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas's most serious challenge — that without a cognizable damages remedy under Cummings, there is nothing for LHEPA to preempt — remains the strongest argument for Respondent, but I find it ultimately unpersuasive for the reasons I articulated in Round 1 and that Justice Kagan reinforces: the preemption inquiry goes to the operative standard of liability, not merely to the remedial tail. Felder v. Casey is instructive precisely because it preempted a state procedural requirement that burdened § 1983 claims even though the underlying remedy was not itself at issue — the structural integrity of the federal cause of action was the operative concern. Justice Alito's mootness point about injunctive relief being prospective deserves acknowledgment, but it goes to whether this is a good vehicle, not to the underlying legal question, and I agree with Justice Roberts that we should resolve this narrowly: LHEPA cannot alter the federal standard of liability for ADA and RA claims, full stop, while leaving damages questions and vehicle-specific concerns to be addressed on remand consistent with Cummings. My textualist methodology requires me to give effect to what Congress actually enacted — a uniform national standard of liability under the ADA and RA — and a state emergency immunity statute that substitutes gross negligence for that standard is in direct conflict with the federal scheme regardless of what remedies ultimately flow from a finding of liability.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas's most serious challenge — that the preemption argument collapses if no cognizable federal remedy exists — retains genuine force, but I am persuaded by the convergent reasoning of Justices Kagan, Gorsuch, and Roberts that the Felder v. Casey framework resolves this concern: preemption analysis goes to the operative elements of the federal cause of action, not merely to available remedies, and Title III's injunctive relief preserves a live controversy sufficient to reach the Supremacy Clause question. Justice Alito's mootness concern about injunctive relief for a discrete past emergency event is the argument I find most troubling at this stage, because if the emergency has ended and prospective injunctive relief is unavailable, the 'live controversy' premise that distinguishes the remedial question from the preemption question may itself be undermined — but this is a vehicle concern about these particular facts rather than a categorical legal objection to the preemption theory. Consistent with my institutionalist approach and Chief Justice Roberts's narrowing formulation, I would hold only that LHEPA cannot displace the federal standard of liability for ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims, explicitly reserving the damages question for remand under Cummings and leaving open the application of LHEPA to purely state law claims — a narrow holding that preserves the Court's institutional credibility while maintaining the structural integrity of federal civil rights law without unnecessarily constraining state emergency authority.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas's most penetrating challenge — that the preemption argument must be tethered to a concrete federal right being displaced, and that the injunctive relief avenue may not have been properly preserved below — retains genuine force under my textualist methodology, and I cannot simply wave it away by invoking the analytical distinction between liability standards and remedies. However, Justice Kagan's Felder v. Casey framework is ultimately more persuasive on the core structural question: Felder held that state procedural requirements were preempted as applied to § 1983 claims because they burdened the vindication of federally guaranteed rights, and LHEPA's imposition of a gross negligence standard on the operative elements of a federal ADA or RA claim — not merely on available remedies — presents the same structural problem regardless of what damages survive Cummings. I share Justice Alito's concern about mootness as applied to injunctive relief for a discrete past emergency event, which is why I would join Chief Justice Roberts's narrowest possible holding: LHEPA cannot alter the federal standard of liability for ADA and RA claims, with all questions about available remedies, mootness, and the adequacy of the record below expressly reserved for remand. This formulation respects the institutional caution Justice Thomas and Justice Alito counsel while preserving the Supremacy Clause's structural function.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas's most serious challenge — that the preemption argument collapses if no cognizable federal remedy exists — remains the strongest opposing argument, but I find it ultimately unpersuasive for reasons that have only been reinforced by this round of deliberation. As Justice Kagan correctly frames it, and as Justice Gorsuch confirms from a textualist methodology, the Felder v. Casey framework establishes that preemption analysis extends to the operative elements of a federal cause of action, not merely to available remedies — a state cannot rewrite what a plaintiff must prove to establish discrimination under federal law, even if what flows from that finding is constrained by Cummings. Justice Alito's mootness concern about injunctive relief deserves acknowledgment: if the emergency event is truly discrete and concluded, prospective injunctive relief may be unavailable on these specific facts, which is why I join Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett in favoring a narrow holding that explicitly reserves the injunctive relief question for remand rather than treating it as definitively established. The structural integrity argument stands independently: allowing states to exploit remedial gaps in federal law to effectively nullify federal liability standards would fall hardest on disabled individuals in emergency contexts — precisely the population Congress most intended to protect — and the Supremacy Clause cannot be read to permit that result.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Supremacy Clause question here is genuinely serious and warrants careful consideration: a state emergency immunity statute that functionally imposes a heightened gross negligence standard on federal disability discrimination claims under Title III of the ADA and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act presents a textbook obstacle preemption problem under Hines v. Davidowitz and its progeny, because Congress established a specific, uniform standard for disability discrimination liability that Louisiana's LHEPA displaces. However, I would resolve this on the narrowest possible grounds — not by broadly invalidating LHEPA, but by holding only that LHEPA cannot be applied to alter the standard of liability for federal civil rights claims, leaving intact its application to state tort and malpractice actions. The respondents' reliance on Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller is not dispositive here because the unavailability of emotional distress damages does not extinguish the underlying federal cause of action or the preemption question regarding the applicable standard of liability. Institutional legitimacy counsels against permitting states to conditionally suspend federal civil rights protections through emergency declarations, as that path would fundamentally undermine the uniform national framework Congress deliberately constructed in the ADA and Rehabilitation Act.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: As an originalist and textualist, I must first address the threshold question of whether Petitioner has a cognizable federal claim that could be preempted. Under Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, 596 U.S., emotional distress damages are categorically unavailable under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act as a matter of Spending Clause contract law, and Title III of the ADA provides no compensatory monetary damages to private plaintiffs at all — only injunctive relief. If no damages remedy exists under federal law in the first instance, there is no federal remedy for LHEPA to displace or preempt, and the Supremacy Clause preemption argument collapses at its foundation. While I acknowledge the serious constitutional concern that a state emergency immunity statute could, in an appropriate case with a viable federal damages claim, constitute obstacle preemption under the Supremacy Clause — and I would be receptive to that argument where a plaintiff actually possesses a cognizable federal remedy — the Petitioner here cannot demonstrate that LHEPA thwarts a federal remedy he never possessed, making dismissal appropriate on these particular facts without reaching the broader preemption question.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: As a textualist, I must first address the threshold issue identified by Respondents: under Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, 596 U.S. (2022), emotional distress damages are categorically unavailable under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, which was enacted pursuant to Congress's Spending Clause authority, and Title III of the ADA similarly does not authorize compensatory damages for private plaintiffs in most circuits. Without available damages, the practical remedy question largely dissolves, and the preemption argument becomes academic. While I acknowledge the Supremacy Clause concern has theoretical merit — states generally cannot impose heightened standards that obstruct federal civil rights enforcement — the Petitioner's failure to identify a cognizable remedy under federal law that LHEPA actually displaced is fatal to the claim; you cannot demonstrate obstacle preemption when the federal statute itself provides no greater relief than what the plaintiff received. Furthermore, the preemption arguments presented below were conclusory and insufficiently developed, and this Court should not grant certiorari to resolve a question that was inadequately briefed and where the underlying federal claim fails on independent grounds regardless of which standard applies.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Supremacy Clause, Art. VI, cl. 2, is unambiguous: state law cannot alter, displace, or impose heightened burdens on the elements of a federal civil rights cause of action. Louisiana's LHEPA, by grafting a gross negligence standard onto ADA Title III and Section 504 claims, fundamentally rewrites the federal statutory framework Congress established — these statutes require intentional discrimination or deliberate indifference, not gross negligence, and a state legislature cannot unilaterally substitute its own fault standard for the one Congress chose. While I take seriously the Respondents' argument under Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller that emotional distress damages are unavailable under Section 504, that damages limitation does not resolve the threshold preemption question of whether LHEPA can categorically alter the liability standard for federal civil rights claims; injunctive and other equitable relief remain available under Title III, preserving a live controversy. The practical stakes for vulnerable populations with disabilities are profound — if states may invoke emergency immunity statutes to conditionally suspend federal civil rights protections during declared emergencies, the ADA and Rehabilitation Act become hollow guarantees precisely when disabled individuals are most at risk, a result Congress could not have intended and the Supremacy Clause forbids.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The core preemption question here is whether Louisiana's LHEPA can impose a heightened gross negligence standard on federal ADA Title III and Section 504 claims without running afoul of the Supremacy Clause. Under Felder v. Casey, 487 U.S. 131 (1988), a state immunity law that thwarts the congressional remedy embedded in a federal civil rights statute is preempted — and LHEPA's functional effect of elevating the plaintiff's burden of proof on a federal discrimination claim does precisely that, regardless of whether the state frames it as tort reform rather than an explicit override of federal law. While Respondents correctly invoke Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller to narrow the available damages under Section 504, that holding does not extinguish the underlying federal cause of action or render the preemption question moot, because Title III's injunctive relief remedies and the structural integrity of federal antidiscrimination law remain at stake; allowing states to conditionally suspend the operative standard of liability for federal civil rights claims during declared emergencies would produce the kind of incoherent, unworkable patchwork that Congress could not have intended when it enacted comprehensive disability rights protections. The pragmatically sound and textually coherent result is to hold that LHEPA cannot displace the federal standard of liability for ADA and RA claims, while acknowledging that Cummings limits the damages recoverable on remand.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: As a textualist and originalist committed to the Supremacy Clause's plain meaning, I find that Louisiana's LHEPA cannot lawfully impose a heightened gross negligence standard on federal ADA Title III and Section 504 claims without running afoul of conflict preemption principles. The text of 42 U.S.C. § 12182 and 29 U.S.C. § 794 establishes specific federal standards for disability discrimination liability, and a state statute that alters the elements a plaintiff must prove to vindicate those federally guaranteed rights stands as an obstacle to the accomplishment of Congress's full purposes — a classic conflict preemption scenario under the Supremacy Clause, Art. VI, cl. 2. While I take seriously the Respondents' argument that Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller forecloses emotional distress damages under Section 504, that remedial limitation does not resolve the threshold structural question of whether a state may categorically rewrite the liability standard for a federal civil rights cause of action, which is a distinct and unresolved federal question of first impression. The rule of lenity and separation of powers concerns cut against permitting states to conditionally suspend federal civil rights protections through temporally triggered emergency statutes, as that would effectively allow state legislatures to override congressional judgments about the scope of federal anti-discrimination law whenever a governor declares an emergency.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Supremacy Clause and foundational conflict preemption doctrine strongly suggest that a state emergency immunity statute cannot alter the elements or burden of proof required to establish a violation of a federal civil rights statute like Title III of the ADA or Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act. When a state law stands as an obstacle to the accomplishment of the full purposes and objectives of Congress in enacting comprehensive federal anti-discrimination protections, it is preempted — and Louisiana's application of LHEPA's gross negligence standard to a federal disability discrimination claim does precisely that by substituting a heightened fault requirement that Congress never imposed. However, I am mindful of the Respondents' serious threshold argument under Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller that emotional distress damages are categorically unavailable under Section 504, which could render the preemption question moot if Petitioner's only cognizable remedy is unavailable regardless of which standard applies — this practical remedial limitation tempers my confidence and counsels careful attention to whether a live, redressable federal claim actually exists before reaching the constitutional preemption question. Consistent with my institutionalist approach favoring judicial restraint and workable rules, I would hold narrowly that LHEPA cannot displace the federal standard of liability for ADA and RA claims while remanding for further consideration of available remedies.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: As a textualist and originalist, I must first address the threshold question of available remedies before reaching the preemption question. Under Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, P.L.L.C., 596 U.S. ___ (2022), emotional distress damages are categorically unavailable to private plaintiffs under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act and, by extension, Title III of the ADA when brought under the Spending Clause framework, which substantially undermines the relief Petitioner seeks. While the Petitioner raises a genuinely serious structural question about whether a state emergency immunity statute can alter the elements of a federal civil rights cause of action — a question that implicates the Supremacy Clause and conflict preemption doctrine — the case as presented may not be the ideal vehicle for resolving that question if the available remedies are so constrained by Cummings as to render the preemption issue largely academic on these facts. The lower courts' application of LHEPA's gross negligence standard to federal ADA and RA claims is analytically troubling and potentially erroneous under conflict preemption principles, but the absence of cognizable damages and the underdeveloped preemption record below counsel in favor of allowing the case to be resolved on the narrower remedial grounds rather than reaching the broader constitutional question at this juncture.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Supremacy Clause, Art. VI, cl. 2, renders state laws that stand as an obstacle to the accomplishment of federal statutory objectives without legal force, and Louisiana's application of LHEPA's heightened gross negligence standard to federal ADA and Section 504 claims constitutes precisely that kind of obstacle preemption — it effectively rewrites the operative elements of a federal civil rights cause of action by grafting on a fault requirement Congress never imposed. Title III of the ADA (42 U.S.C. § 12182) and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act (29 U.S.C. § 794) establish uniform national standards for disability discrimination that do not condition liability on gross negligence, and permitting states to impose heightened standards during declared emergencies would render federal civil rights protections contingent and non-uniform in precisely the circumstances where vulnerable populations most need them. While I take seriously the Respondents' argument under Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller that emotional distress damages are categorically unavailable under Section 504, that remedial limitation does not resolve the antecedent preemption question of whether the state standard of liability itself was lawfully applied to the federal claim — the two inquiries are analytically distinct. My background as a public defender reinforces my concern that allowing emergency immunity statutes to swallow federal civil rights protections creates accountability gaps that fall disproportionately on disabled individuals and other marginalized groups who depend most heavily on federal statutory guarantees.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Louisiana's Healthcare Emergency Powers Act (LHEPA), a state COVID-19 emergency immunity statute, can lawfully displace or preempt federal disability discrimination claims brought under Title III of the ADA and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act by imposing a heightened gross negligence standard not required under federal law.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Louisiana Healthcare Emergency Powers Act (LHEPA); Title III of the Americans with Disabilities Act (42 U.S.C. § 12182); Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 (29 U.S.C. § 794); Supremacy Clause, U.S. Const. Art. VI, cl. 2
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner John Doe argues that the Louisiana courts erred by applying LHEPA's heightened gross negligence standard to his federal ADA and RA disability discrimination claims, effectively nullifying federally guaranteed civil rights protections through a state emergency immunity statute. He contends that federal law preempts LHEPA as applied to federal civil rights claims, that the Supremacy Clause prohibits states from conditioning or displacing federal antidiscrimination mandates through state procedural immunity laws, and that allowing states to invoke emergency statutes to preclude ADA and RA claims creates dangerous precedent undermining uniform national enforcement of federal disability rights. He further argues this presents a pure, unresolved question of federal law warranting Supreme Court review.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents Dynamic Physical Therapy, LLC and Scott Newton argue that the petition rests on a false premise because monetary compensatory emotional distress damages are categorically unavailable to private plaintiffs under Title III of the ADA and Section 504 of the RA following the Supreme Court's decision in Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, rendering the federal claims legally deficient regardless of LHEPA's application. They further contend that Petitioner's preemption arguments were conclusory, unsupported by facts, and cited no legal authority in the lower courts, and that the Louisiana courts correctly applied LHEPA given that the denial of aquatic physical therapy occurred during the declared COVID-19 public health emergency in December 2020.

Doe v. Dynamic Physical Therapy, LLC, 407 So.3d 623 (La. 2025) — Louisiana Supreme Court denial of certiorari with Griffin, J. dissent

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument that the complaint's pleading of the preemption question may have implicitly encompassed declaratory relief sufficient to preserve a live controversy is the most serious challenge to my position, and I acknowledge it has genuine force — if injunctive or declaratory relief was reasonably implied, the Cummings foreclosure does not extinguish the federal cause of action and the preemption question is not advisory. However, my minimalist instincts remain dispositive: even crediting Justice Barrett's charitable reading of the complaint, Justice Kavanaugh's preservation concern is independently sufficient to counsel restraint, because we would be resolving a significant Supremacy Clause federalism question about state emergency immunity statutes and federal disability law on a record where the obstacle preemption argument was inadequately developed below. Justice Kagan's suggestion of a GVR with instructions to clarify the remedial record is actually the disposition that most appeals to my judicial philosophy — it addresses the vehicle concerns without issuing an advisory opinion or permanently foreclosing the preemption question — but since that option is not commanding a majority, I maintain my position that dismissal or a narrow ruling on threshold grounds is preferable to a broad Supremacy Clause holding on this record. As Chief Justice, I would note that a narrower holding limited to the specific remedial deficiency, expressly reserving the preemption question for a cleaner vehicle, might attract Justices Kagan and Barrett and produce a more institutionally legitimate outcome than either a broad merits ruling or a bare dismissal.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument that injunctive relief may have been 'pleaded or reasonably implied' is the most serious challenge to my position, but I cannot accept it as a basis for reaching the Supremacy Clause question because federal courts adjudicate the case as actually presented, not as it might have been better presented. Justice Jackson's contention that my position 'proves too much' by conflating unavailability of one remedy with extinguishment of the entire cause of action is intellectually serious, but it founders on the same rock: the original public meaning of Article III's case-or-controversy requirement demands that a plaintiff demonstrate a concrete, redressable injury based on relief actually sought, not relief theoretically available in a better-pleaded complaint. Justice Sotomayor's Felder v. Casey argument remains the most powerful originalist challenge — the Supremacy Clause's original meaning does forbid states from using procedural devices to nullify federal rights — but Felder's force presupposes a viable federal remedy actually being displaced in the litigation before the Court, and that predicate is not satisfied when the plaintiff sought only emotional distress damages that Cummings categorically forecloses. I maintain my position that the Court should await a cleaner vehicle where injunctive relief is actually sought, the preemption argument is fully developed below, and the record unambiguously presents the Supremacy Clause question.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan both argue that Cummings does not extinguish the entire federal cause of action because injunctive relief remains available under Title III, which they contend preserves the live preemption question. However, this argument fails on the record before us: Petitioner never sought injunctive relief — the complaint sought only compensatory damages for emotional distress, which Cummings categorically forecloses. A federal claim without a cognizable remedy on the facts as pleaded is not a live federal claim that can generate a preemption conflict; it is a legally deficient claim that should be dismissed on threshold grounds. Justice Kagan's pragmatic concern about a patchwork of enforcement is genuinely serious and might be compelling in a properly presented case where the plaintiff sought injunctive relief, but we cannot manufacture a better vehicle from this record, and issuing a broad Supremacy Clause ruling on the basis of a remedy Petitioner never requested would produce precisely the kind of advisory opinion that Article III forbids.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito's threshold argument — that Petitioner sought only emotional distress damages foreclosed by Cummings, leaving no live federal remedy — remains the strongest challenge to my position, but I continue to find it unpersuasive for reasons Justice Jackson articulates with particular force: conflating the unavailability of one damages category with extinguishment of the entire federal cause of action misreads both Cummings and Title III's remedial structure. Injunctive and declaratory relief remain available, and LHEPA's gross negligence threshold would still operate as an obstacle to those remedies — a plaintiff seeking prospective relief from a covered entity cannot obtain it if the state has immunized that entity absent a showing of gross negligence, which is precisely the kind of state law that Felder v. Casey's Supremacy Clause logic condemns. Justice Barrett's honest acknowledgment that the record may not clearly establish Petitioner sought only damages to the exclusion of all other relief reinforces my view that the vehicle problem is overstated. The deeper structural concern driving my position is that accepting the Respondents' threshold argument teaches states that emergency immunity statutes can effectively nullify federal civil rights frameworks whenever damages are constrained — a lesson that falls hardest on people with disabilities who depend on federal law as their primary protection against discriminatory treatment in healthcare settings.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito's threshold argument remains the most formidable challenge to my position — if Petitioner genuinely sought only emotional distress damages foreclosed by Cummings, then pointing to injunctive relief as preserving the controversy does risk manufacturing a better vehicle from a deficient record, which my textualist commitments resist. But I keep returning to Justice Barrett's honest acknowledgment that the record may not conclusively establish this, and to Justice Jackson's structural point that LHEPA's gross negligence threshold would obstruct injunctive relief just as surely as damages relief — meaning the preemption conflict is real regardless of which remedy form we examine. What ultimately holds me at Petitioner, though with diminished confidence, is that the Respondents' vehicle argument, if accepted, would teach states that emergency immunity statutes can permanently overlay federal disability rights whenever one damages category is constrained by a subsequent Supreme Court ruling like Cummings — a structural consequence that Felder v. Casey's Supremacy Clause logic was precisely designed to prevent. I remain open to a GVR disposition that clarifies the remedial record below, which would address Justice Kavanaugh's legitimate preservation concerns without either issuing an advisory opinion or permanently foreclosing the preemption question.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Barrett's argument that injunctive relief may have been 'pleaded or reasonably implied' is the most serious challenge to my position, but it ultimately fails under my textualist methodology: we adjudicate the case as actually pleaded and litigated, not as it might have been pleaded. Justice Jackson's contention that I am conflating unavailability of one remedy with extinguishment of the entire cause of action is intellectually serious, but the Article III case-or-controversy requirement demands that a plaintiff have a cognizable remedy for the specific injury alleged — and here, the only injury Petitioner actually sought to remedy through the only relief actually requested is categorically foreclosed by Cummings. Justice Sotomayor's Felder v. Casey argument would be compelling in a case where a plaintiff with a viable federal remedy faces state immunity obstruction, but Felder's Supremacy Clause logic presupposes a live federal claim with available relief, not a theoretical claim reconstructed from remedies never sought. I remain firm that issuing a broad obstacle preemption ruling in this vehicle would constitute precisely the advisory opinion Article III forbids, and the Court should await a plaintiff who seeks injunctive relief, develops the preemption argument below, and presents a clean record.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan's suggestion of a GVR with instructions to clarify the remedial record below is the most intellectually honest response to the genuine uncertainty Justice Barrett identifies about whether Petitioner sought only emotional distress damages — and I find it more persuasive than either a full merits ruling for Petitioner or a clean dismissal. However, even accepting that a GVR might be appropriate, my institutionalist concerns about the inadequate preservation of the preemption argument in the lower courts remain independently dispositive: the obstacle preemption theory was not fully developed below, and reaching a significant Supremacy Clause federalism question about state emergency immunity statutes on this record would undermine the Court's legitimacy regardless of how the remedial ambiguity is resolved. Justice Jackson's structural point — that accepting the vehicle argument teaches states they can deploy emergency immunity statutes to nullify federal disability rights during declared emergencies — is genuinely compelling and might be decisive in a properly presented vehicle, but the answer to that concern is disciplined restraint now in favor of a cleaner case, not stretching Article III to reach a significant constitutional question on a deficient record. I maintain my position for Respondent, though I would support a GVR disposition over outright dismissal if that is where the Court's majority coalesces.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito and Justice Gorsuch press the vehicle problem with genuine force, and I continue to take seriously the textualist principle that we adjudicate the case as actually pleaded rather than as it might have been better presented. However, the argument that most moves me toward maintaining my position is Justice Jackson's structural point — that LHEPA's gross negligence threshold operates as a substantive obstacle to the federal cause of action regardless of remedy form, because a court cannot grant injunctive relief against a defendant immunized from liability absent that heightened showing. Justice Kavanaugh's preservation concern remains the most intellectually honest version of the Respondents' position, and I acknowledge that a GVR with instructions to clarify the remedial record below might be the most defensible disposition — but I am not persuaded the preservation defect is so complete as to foreclose the merits entirely, particularly given that the Supremacy Clause question was at least raised below even if not fully developed. The combination of the complaint's potentially ambiguous prayer for relief and the structural Felder v. Casey logic that states cannot use immunity statutes to raise the substantive fault threshold Congress deliberately set keeps me, with modest confidence, on Petitioner's side.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the vehicle problem most forcefully — that Petitioner never sought injunctive relief, so there is no live federal remedy being displaced and the preemption question becomes advisory. But I cannot accept this framing for a reason Justice Sotomayor identifies with precision: LHEPA's gross negligence threshold would obstruct injunctive relief as well as damages, because a court cannot grant prospective relief against a defendant who is immunized from liability absent a showing of gross negligence — that is a substantive obstacle to the federal cause of action regardless of the remedy's form. The deeper flaw in the Respondents' vehicle argument is that it treats Petitioner's litigation choices about which remedy to emphasize as extinguishing the underlying federal cause of action itself, which conflates remedy selection with claim viability in a way that Felder v. Casey's logic squarely rejects. Justice Kavanaugh's preservation concern is the most honest version of the Respondents' position, and I acknowledge it has some force, but inadequate preservation below is a basis for a GVR rather than a ruling that state emergency immunity statutes may constitutionally overlay federal disability rights — and I would not allow a preservation defect to become a permanent license for states to nullify the ADA during declared emergencies.

John Roberts.reasoning: While the preemption question raised by Petitioner is genuinely serious and implicates core Supremacy Clause concerns — particularly given Felder v. Casey's holding that states cannot apply their own procedural rules to defeat federal civil rights claims — my minimalist approach counsels resolving this case on the narrowest available ground. Respondents correctly identify that Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller (2022) forecloses the only damages remedy Petitioner sought, namely compensatory emotional distress damages, rendering the federal claims legally deficient independent of LHEPA's application. Because the federal claims fail on their own terms under controlling Supreme Court precedent, there is no need to reach the broader and admittedly complex conflict preemption question, and issuing an advisory ruling on LHEPA's preemption when the underlying federal remedy is unavailable would exceed the narrow judicial role I believe this Court should occupy. Institutional legitimacy is best served by declining to resolve a significant federalism question when an antecedent, case-dispositive ground exists.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: As an originalist, I must first address the threshold question of whether Petitioner's federal claims are legally viable before reaching the preemption question. Under Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller (2022), emotional distress damages are categorically unavailable under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act and analogous Spending Clause statutes, which fatally undermines the relief Petitioner seeks and renders the preemption question largely academic in this vehicle. Furthermore, while the Supremacy Clause's original public meaning — as understood by the Founders and reflected in the debates of the Constitutional Convention — does establish federal law as supreme over conflicting state law, the preemption argument here was not properly preserved below with adequate legal authority or factual development, making this a poor vehicle for resolving the important federal question presented. I would be deeply skeptical of LHEPA's application to federal civil rights claims in a properly presented case, as states cannot through procedural immunity statutes effectively nullify congressionally enacted federal rights, but the deficiencies in Petitioner's damages theory and preservation of arguments counsel in favor of the Respondent here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: As a textualist focused on practical consequences, I find the threshold question dispositive: Petitioner's federal claims are legally defective regardless of LHEPA's application. Under Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, 596 U.S. 212 (2022), emotional distress damages are categorically unavailable under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, and the well-established circuit consensus confirms monetary damages are not available in private suits under Title III of the ADA — only prospective injunctive relief is cognizable, which Petitioner never sought. Because Petitioner's federal claims could not have survived in any forum at any time, the preemption and Supremacy Clause questions regarding LHEPA's heightened gross negligence standard are entirely academic — there is no viable federal remedy being displaced. Granting certiorari to resolve a constitutional preemption question when the underlying federal claims are facially defective would be a misuse of this Court's resources and would produce an advisory opinion on an abstract legal question, contrary to sound judicial practice.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Supremacy Clause and conflict preemption doctrine compel the conclusion that Louisiana's LHEPA cannot lawfully impose a heightened gross negligence standard on federal ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims, because doing so frustrates the purposes and objectives of Congress in enacting uniform national antidiscrimination protections for people with disabilities. As established in Felder v. Casey, 487 U.S. 131 (1988), a state immunity law that thwarts the congressional remedy embedded in a federal civil rights statute is preempted, and importing a fault standard foreign to the federal cause of action effectively nullifies the federal right in state court proceedings. While I take seriously the Respondents' argument that Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller forecloses emotional distress damages under Section 504, that holding does not extinguish the entire federal cause of action — injunctive relief and other remedies remain available under Title III, and the LHEPA's application to those claims still impermissibly displaces federal law. Allowing states to invoke emergency immunity statutes to condition or heighten the standards governing federal civil rights claims creates precisely the kind of accountability gap that falls hardest on vulnerable populations — people with disabilities who depend on consistent, enforceable federal protections regardless of whether a public health crisis has been declared.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Supremacy Clause analysis here closely tracks Felder v. Casey's core holding that state procedural rules cannot be applied to federal civil rights claims when they materially burden the vindication of federally-created rights — LHEPA's heightened gross negligence standard does precisely that by effectively immunizing conduct that would otherwise constitute actionable disability discrimination under Title III of the ADA and Section 504. While Respondents raise a serious threshold argument under Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller regarding the unavailability of emotional distress damages, that ruling does not categorically extinguish all relief available under Title III or Section 504, as injunctive relief and other remedies remain viable, meaning the federal claims are not legally deficient on their face and the preemption question retains live significance. The workability concern that animates my pragmatic approach cuts strongly against permitting states to deploy emergency immunity statutes as a variable overlay on federal antidiscrimination mandates — doing so would produce the precisely unworkable patchwork of enforcement that Congress sought to foreclose through uniform national disability rights law, with outcomes turning arbitrarily on forum selection rather than the merits of the federal claim. That said, I would cabin the holding narrowly: LHEPA is preempted only as applied to federal ADA and RA claims, leaving the statute fully operative for state tort claims, consistent with the principle that conflict preemption should be no broader than necessary to vindicate the federal statutory purpose.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: As a textualist, I must begin with what Congress actually authorized as remedies under Title III of the ADA and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act. Following Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller (2022), emotional distress damages are categorically unavailable under these statutes because Congress, when it conditioned federal funding and enacted these provisions, did not unambiguously authorize such relief — meaning Petitioner's federal claims lack a cognizable remedy regardless of how LHEPA is applied. Without a viable federal remedy on the merits, the preemption question — however genuinely interesting as an abstract matter of Supremacy Clause doctrine — becomes an advisory opinion on a hypothetical conflict, which Article III forbids me from issuing. The obstacle preemption argument under Hines v. Davidowitz is intellectually serious and might prevail in a case where the underlying federal claim carries an available remedy, but this is not that case, and I will not manufacture federal jurisdiction to reach a constitutional question when the statutory predicate fails.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: While the preemption question raised by Petitioner is genuinely serious and the Supremacy Clause concerns about states using emergency immunity statutes to nullify federal civil rights protections are not frivolous, the threshold problem identified by Respondents under Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, 596 U.S. 212 (2022) is dispositive at this juncture. Because Cummings forecloses emotional distress damages under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act and Title III of the ADA for private plaintiffs, Petitioner's federal claims lack a viable remedy regardless of whether LHEPA's heightened gross negligence standard is preempted, making this a poor vehicle for resolving the broader preemption question. My institutionalist concern for judicial restraint counsels against reaching a significant constitutional preemption ruling when the underlying federal claims are legally deficient on independent grounds, and the record reflects that Petitioner's preemption arguments were inadequately developed in the lower courts. The Court should await a cleaner vehicle where the federal claims are legally sound before addressing whether state COVID-19 emergency immunity statutes can constitutionally displace federal disability discrimination mandates under the obstacle preemption framework of Hines v. Davidowitz.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Applying conflict preemption analysis under the Supremacy Clause, Art. VI, cl. 2, a state immunity statute that imports a heightened gross negligence standard into a federal civil rights cause of action under Title III of the ADA (42 U.S.C. § 12182) and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act (29 U.S.C. § 794) stands as an obstacle to the accomplishment of Congress's remedial purposes and is therefore preempted. The original public meaning of the Supremacy Clause, combined with this Court's holdings in Felder v. Casey, 487 U.S. 131 (1988), and Howlett v. Rose, 496 U.S. 356 (1990), establishes that state courts adjudicating federal claims may not impose state-law procedural or immunity obstacles that effectively nullify the federal right — LHEPA's gross negligence threshold does precisely that by altering the elements of liability Congress prescribed. While Respondents correctly note that Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller, 596 U.S. 212 (2022), forecloses emotional distress damages under Section 504 and Title III, this damages limitation does not extinguish the underlying federal cause of action or render the preemption question moot, as injunctive relief and other remedies may remain available and the structural question of whether states may condition federal civil rights claims through emergency immunity statutes warrants resolution. I write with measured confidence because the Cummings damages issue and the adequacy of Petitioner's preservation of the preemption argument below introduce genuine threshold questions that could independently dispose of the case without reaching the merits.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Supremacy Clause and conflict preemption doctrine, as articulated in Hines v. Davidowitz and its progeny, compel the conclusion that LHEPA cannot lawfully impose a heightened gross negligence standard on federal ADA Title III and Section 504 claims, because doing so stands as a direct obstacle to Congress's full purposes and objectives in enacting comprehensive, uniform federal disability antidiscrimination protections. When a state procedural or immunity statute effectively raises the substantive threshold of liability for federal civil rights claims — transforming a negligence-based federal standard into a gross negligence requirement — it does not merely regulate procedure but displaces the federally guaranteed right itself, which is precisely the kind of state interference the Supremacy Clause prohibits. While Respondents raise a legitimate threshold concern under Cummings v. Premier Rehab Keller regarding the unavailability of emotional distress damages under Section 504 and Title III, that damages limitation does not categorically extinguish all available relief under these statutes, including injunctive relief and nominal damages, meaning the federal claims retain independent vitality that LHEPA cannot constitutionally nullify. My background as a public defender and commitment to procedural fairness reinforces my concern that permitting states to invoke emergency immunity statutes to categorically foreclose federal civil rights adjudication would create dangerous, unequal enforcement of disability rights depending solely on the forum in which a claim is brought, undermining the uniform national mandate Congress deliberately established.
